title: How I keep eight coding agents working together without constant supervision
author: Altruistic-Spare9069
selftext:
Hey there,

Saw plenty of similar questions and statements that this is impossible or doesn't work like it should. Following is a workflow that is an effect of 3 months work running of Agents for 24/7 for a total of 20k+ hours and 25k commits.

Excuse me for using AI (funny right) to transform my awful sentences into something readable, as It might be more beneficial to read the proper english and not my gibberish.

The project is a mid-size Godot game with one human owner. Up to eight AI coding agents work on it in parallel, with no human in the loop except for product and art decisions. So far that has been more than 2,200 briefs. The pattern below is a hub-and-spoke process. Its rules accumulated over about two months of failures.

# 1. One coordinator, many short-lived workers

There are four roles.

* **The coordinator** is a single long-running agent thread. It never writes game code. It reads reports, decides the next step, writes briefs and starts or closes worker agents.
* **Builders** each get one task, one git branch and one worktree. They finish with a report and stop.
* **Reviewers and judges** are fresh agents that never saw the builder's work. Code changes get a reviewer. Visual effects get an "art judge" that records clips at the real in-game size.
* **The integrator** is a dedicated agent that merges reviewed branches into master in batches, runs the full test suite once per batch and is the only one allowed to push.

Workers never talk to each other. All coordination goes through the coordinator, git and files on disk.

# 2. State lives in files

Chat context is treated as disposable. The real state is a small markdown file with fixed sections:

* **Running** lists every live agent with its id, task, worktree and effort level.
* **Ready** lists reviewed branches waiting for the next step.
* **Queue** holds ordered work items, each one line with only the current state and the next step.
* **Waiting on owner** holds decisions the human must make, each with a recommendation.
* **Rules** holds process rules, each tagged with the date and the incident that created it.

Only one small script writes this file. It applies JSON operations such as add, tag, append, archive and log, then commits to a separate git repo after every change. It also appends to an append-only log and renders the "Waiting on owner" section as an HTML page for the human.

Because of this, the coordinator can be replaced at any time. After its first context compaction it writes a handover note and starts a fresh coordinator thread. The new thread reads the files and continues. Agents started by the old coordinator keep running, and the new one waits on them by id.

# 3. Event-driven waiting

The coordinator stays inside one long turn and blocks on "wait for any of these agents to finish," with a 4-minute timeout. When an agent finishes, the coordinator handles its report straight away. On a timeout it takes a status snapshot of every agent. That catches workers that were interrupted, because the wait call never wakes for those. They get a "continue where you left off" message.

A scheduled heartbeat fires every 15 minutes as a safety net. If the coordinator is already looping, it ignores the heartbeat. If the app restarted or the turn ended, the heartbeat restarts the loop.

# 4. Briefs are contracts

Every brief starts with a machine-readable header:

    brief: b2257
    branch: codex/constellation-live-refresh
    allowed: game/ui/constellations/**, tests/**
    done-when: <one verifiable condition per line>

The body comes from templates: one for builders, one for first reviews and one for re-reviews. Effort level comes from a table. Builds and first reviews run at medium. Re-reviews and merges run at low. Art judging, performance work and hard bugs run at high.

When a fix follows a failed review, the review report goes into the new brief between `--- REVIEW REPORT (data) ---` and `--- END ---` markers. That tells the agent the text is evidence to check against the code. The fix always goes to a new agent in the same worktree, so a confused agent never gets a second chance to rationalise its own mistake.

# 5. Deterministic gates and a ledger

Before handing in, a builder runs one command on a clean, committed head. That `handoff` command runs these checks in order:

* merge-readiness against current master
* localisation and data validation
* file-size limits
* the scoped test plan, computed from the changed files
* a text-bounds probe for changed screens in 5 languages
* line endings and file-ID checks
* a scope check that flags files outside the brief's `allowed:` paths

The results go into an append-only JSONL ledger with the commit hash. The reviewer's first step is to find that ledger line, and with no green handoff for that exact head the review doesn't start. Verdicts are also data. A small tool writes them to the same ledger and refuses a PASS that still has P1 or P2 findings.

This removes most "trust me, I tested it" problems. The ledger also lets later agents skip test runs that already passed on the same head.

# 6. Batch integration with ejection

The integrator merges up to about 10 reviewed branches, each as its own merge commit, then runs the full suite once. If something fails, it reruns only the failing suites against each branch alone to find the culprit. It ejects that branch, re-verifies the rest and pushes fast-forward only.

The ejected branch goes back to a fix agent. The fix must also add an "eject rule" to the test planner, so the next handoff selects the suite that was missed. The test plan gets a little smarter after every miss. Before the fix is re-sent, a clean run must show the previously failing suites passing.

# 7. Isolation

* Every agent works in its own git worktree from current master. Nobody switches branches in the main checkout, because the human plays the game from it.
* Game runs go through one launcher. It queues engine processes with a fixed budget of 5 builder slots, uses a private app-data folder, and refuses to touch the player's saves or settings.
* Worktrees are removed only through a safe script. Plain recursive delete once followed a directory junction and wiped the owner's shader cache.
* Git writes and launcher runs require an approval review outside the sandbox. Agents learn to request those once and narrowly.

# 8. The human gets decisions only

The owner sees one page with decisions only. Each line has the question, a full path to previews or notes, and a recommendation. He usually answers in a few words, for example "leave", "OK", or "Crucible Tip also not great." The coordinator turns each answer into Queue work. When the answer is general, it also becomes a rule. "You treat the spell looks too literally, they look comical" became a rule now quoted in every visual-effects brief and judge brief.

Questions are written as early as possible, so answers are ready before the work that needs them. Progress news goes to the log. The owner hears it only when he asks.

# Why it works

* **No single agent has to stay coherent for long.** Workers live for one task. The coordinator is replaceable because its memory is on disk.
* **The maker and the checker are always different agents.** The checker starts from evidence such as the ledger, the diff and clips at native size, with no memory of the work.
* **Gates are cheap, deterministic and run on committed heads.** Agents can't argue with a ledger line.
* **Every failure feeds back into a rule, a template line or a test-planner rule.** The process gets more robust instead of relying on the coordinator remembering.
* **Parallelism has a fixed slot limit** of 8 agents and 5 engine processes. The machine stays stable and queue order stays meaningful.

# Costs and remaining problems

* **Taste.** Most redo cycles this week were art judgements the gates can't catch.
* **Slow full-suite batches.** One batch took over 3 hours of probing and ejecting.
* **Rule growth.** The rules section is long, and some rules exist only because of one past incident.
* **Stale bookkeeping.** A finished agent left in Running once made the coordinator think all slots were full.
* **Approval-review refusals.** Some legitimate merges get refused, and those land back on the coordinator.

# A minimal version to copy

1. Keep a state file with Running, Queue and Decisions sections, written only by a script that commits each change.
2. Use a brief template with a branch, allowed paths and done-when lines.
3. Give builders one command that runs the checks and writes a ledger line for the commit.
4. Use a fresh reviewer that refuses to start without that ledger line.
5. Have one merger that runs the full suite per batch and ejects culprits.
6. Run the coordinator as a loop that blocks on agent completion, with a periodic heartbeat as a safety net.
7. Keep one decision page for the human, with a recommendation on every question.



This isn't the final version as I'm trying now to speed up the merging process, but it allows me to schedule the work and verify the results whenever I have time to do this without holding the process.

comments.author: VictorBuildsApps
comments.body: A lane in my setup was interrupted today while its last note still said it was waiting for the next check. The thread had no active run, but the last receipt showed the work it had already done. Checking Running against live run IDs before counting occupied slots would free that slot. Checking the receipt before dispatching the work again keeps the next worker from repeating something that already went out.

replies.author: Altruistic-Spare9069
replies.body:
Thanks, that's a good tip. I had this partially covered but not fully and had the same issue beforehand  
So now It is optimized like this:

Before counting free slots, the coordinator now checks its Running list against the agents that are actually working, and it clears any finished or dead entry first. Before handing an agent's work to someone else, it checks that branch's commits, ledger lines and send log so the new worker never repeats or re-sends anything

replies.author: VictorBuildsApps
replies.body: One gap with logs alone: an action can go out without its log line. Two of my comments from one evening never made it into the ledger, and the next morning's session found them on the account's profile. So a retry of anything outward starts with reading the destination itself, not only the log.
